clue.text: Repulsive manoeuvre by bishop blocking stipend?

indicators.note: to block a road is to stand in the middle of it, so one piece blocking another sits inside it

parts.note: a stipend is a clergyman's pay
a bishop is styled the Right Reverend, RR

explanation.surface: A bishop pulls some disgusting stunt to get between a vicar and his living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repulsive' reads as 'disgusting', but it is doing its older job of 'repelling': the manoeuvre drives a blow away. Stipend and bishop keep the whole scene in the Church.
explanation.definitionFit: A parry is a fencer's or boxer's move that turns an attack aside, so it is literally a manoeuvre that repulses.

clue.text: Trouble over stag do attendees getting into scrap in Hooters

definitions.note: A plural noun can stand for a collective one: parliament is the name for a group of owls, so it means 'hooters' taken together.

indicators.note: to turn something over is to flip it, so the word is reversed
something getting into another is going inside it

parts.note: a scrap of something is a part of it
to trouble is to ail, and AIL is turned over
a stag do is an all-male pre-wedding party

explanation.surface: A stag party gets into a fight at Hooters, the American restaurant chain.
explanation.walkthrough: Hooters is the restaurant chain, and a scrap there sounds like a brawl; really hooters are owls and the scrap is a piece. A stag do is the British name for a bachelor party.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament is the collective noun for owls, the birds that hoot.

clue.text: Account of part of canal containing island

indicators.note: to contain something is to hold it inside

parts.note: rectal means of the rectum, the last part of the alimentary canal
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A report on a stretch of canal that has an island in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The canal reads as a waterway with an island, but it is the alimentary canal. 'Account of' misleads too: 'of' belongs with the wordplay, since rectal means 'of the rectum'.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a detailed telling of facts, as in a recital of grievances, so it is an account.

clue.text: I'd like that contract after years with fantastic talent

indicators.note: one piece coming after the others is placed behind them

parts.note: Y is the standard abbreviation for years
extrasensory perception, ESP, is a talent from fantasy
a lease is a rental contract

explanation.surface: An agent eyeing a contract for a long-serving and fantastically talented client.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic talent' sounds like praise, but it means a talent from fantasy, such as mind-reading. The contract arrives first in the clue and last in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Yes please' is how you accept an offer, so it says exactly 'I’d like that'.

clue.text: He wrote why grim seaman struggles, after A Farewell to Arms in novel form

indicators.note: something that struggles thrashes about, so these letters are thrown out of their order
to bid farewell to something is to see it leave, so the letters named next depart
a novel form is a new shape, so the departing letters leave scattered rather than as one word

parts.note: the letters of WHY GRIM SEAMAN, stirred up once four have gone
A, R, M and S are the letters removed, picked out from wherever they sit

explanation.surface: A literary puzzle about the author of a novel on a grim seaman's struggles, written after A Farewell to Arms.
explanation.walkthrough: ARMS does not sit together in WHY GRIM SEAMAN, which is why the clue says 'in novel form': you delete its letters one by one before shuffling. The Old Man and the Sea, the grim seaman's struggle, did follow A Farewell to Arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway wrote A Farewell to Arms and The Old Man and the Sea, so 'He wrote' is the man himself described by his trade.

clue.text: Country song that's done well, claiming American #1

indicators.note: to claim something is to take it for yourself, so the word takes the next piece inside it

parts.note: a hit is a song that does well in the charts
A is the standard abbreviation for American
number one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A country music single that's been a success, claiming the top spot in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country song' reads as a genre, but Country is the definition on its own. 'American #1' looks like a chart position; it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiti is a Caribbean country, so this is a definition by category.

clue.text: Vegetable — people beat it

parts.note: to people a place is to man it, to supply it with staff
'beat it!' is a rude way of saying 'get out!'

explanation.surface: A cry against vegetables: people, beat them!
explanation.walkthrough: 'People' looks like a plural noun, but it is the verb: to people a ship is to man it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mangetout is a pea eaten pod and all, a vegetable known in America as the snow pea.

clue.text: Piece that should be exactly fitting for 9?

indicators.note: 9 across is RECESSION, a going back, so putting the word through a recession reverses it

parts.note: a tenon is the tongue of wood cut to fit a mortise exactly, and TENON goes backwards

explanation.surface: A jigsaw piece that ought to fit perfectly into slot 9.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference does double duty: 9 is the number of players a nonet is written for, and 9 across supplies the reversal. A tenon and mortise is the carpenter's classic tight joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a piece of music for nine performers, so 'Piece' is the definition and 'for 9' confirms it.

clue.text: Midlands town where match may be held following some fighting

indicators.note: what comes following another comes after it, so this piece goes second

parts.note: war is fighting on a large scale
a wick is where a flame is held, like a lit match

explanation.surface: A Midlands town where a sports match might be staged after some brawling.
explanation.walkthrough: The match looks like a sporting fixture, but it is the one you strike: a flame sits on a candle's wick.
explanation.definitionFit: Warwick is the county town of Warwickshire in England's West Midlands, famous for its castle.

clue.text: Plaything repeatedly going up and down time and time again?

definitions.text: Plaything repeatedly going up and down time and time again?

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means read from the bottom, so the word is reversed
down means less, so the letters named next are taken away

parts.note: a plaything is a TOY, written twice and reversed
time is T, and one T goes from each half

explanation.surface: A description of a toy that goes up and down over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the whole clue describes the toy; read as instructions, 'up and down' splits into a reversal and a subtraction. 'Time and time again' is two Ts.
explanation.definitionFit: A yo-yo is a toy spun up and down its string over and over, so the whole clue is a plain description of it.

clue.text: Consecutive GDP falls and rises once sorted out

indicators.note: to sort something out is to rearrange it into a new order

parts.note: RISES ONCE rearranged

explanation.surface: An economist's note on a run of GDP falls followed by rises that sorted things out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls and rises' looks like one economic phrase, but the definition stops at 'falls' and 'rises' is fodder. The economists' rule of thumb is two quarters of shrinking output in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A recession is conventionally defined as two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, so the definition is the textbook one.

clue.text: Queen and duke wearing Nancy's coat like an anorak

indicators.note: whoever is wearing something has it wrapped round them, so the pieces before it go inside
a coat is the outside layer, so only the outer letters of the word are used

parts.note: the outside letters of NancY
Elizabeth Regina, ER
D is the standard abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A queen and a duke borrow Nancy's coat, which turns out to be an anorak.
explanation.walkthrough: The anorak looks like a garment to go with 'coat', but it is the British slang for an obsessive enthusiast. 'Nancy’s coat' is only her outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang an anorak is a socially awkward obsessive, the sort who wore one trainspotting, so 'like an anorak' means nerdy.

clue.text: One eating lentils, nuts and Smarties

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, and crazy letters do not stay in their proper order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
EATING LENTILS rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone snacking on lentils, nuts and chocolate sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S makes 'Smarties' look like the chocolate sweets, and 'nuts' looks like another snack in the list. Smarties are clever people and nuts is telling you to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The intelligentsia are a society's intellectual class, and 'smarties' is a jokey plural for clever people.

clue.text: Reason to keep uncle dancing for TikToker?

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places
to keep something is to hold it, so the next piece goes inside

parts.note: to infer is to reason something out
UNCLE rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone justifies an uncle's dancing by saying it is for TikTok.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle dancing for TikTok is a real genre of video, which is why the surface holds together. 'Reason' is the verb, to work something out.
explanation.definitionFit: An influencer is a social-media personality paid to sway followers, and TikTok is one of their platforms, so the question mark flags a definition by example.

clue.text: Batter rejected by Fat Duck

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word goes backwards

parts.note: to lam is to batter, and LAM goes backwards
lard is pig fat

explanation.surface: A batter turned away by the Fat Duck, Heston Blumenthal's famous restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' pulls towards cooking because the Fat Duck is a restaurant, but it is the verb: to lam someone is to thrash them. 'Fat Duck' splits into wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The mallard is the commonest wild duck, the green-headed ancestor of most farmyard breeds, so this is a definition by example.

clue.text: Advert regularly positions brushes?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the even letters of aDvErT
a position on a question is an angle on it

explanation.surface: An advert keeps placing hairbrushes in shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brushes' looks like a plural noun, but it is the verb: someone who brushes hair works the knots out.
explanation.definitionFit: Brushing hair works the knots out of it, so brushes means detangles; the question mark admits brushing is only one way to do it.

clue.text: Material works excluding First Blood

indicators.note: excluding the first means leaving out the opening letter

parts.note: to work is to toil, and TOILS loses its first letter T
blood relations are kin

explanation.surface: A film critic's note on material from Stallone's works that leaves out First Blood.
explanation.walkthrough: First Blood is the first Rambo film, so the words look glued together, but 'First' belongs to the indicator and 'Blood' stands alone as family.
explanation.definitionFit: Oilskin is cotton cloth waterproofed with oil, a material for sailors' coats.

clue.text: Publisher of fake news easily influenced, powerless to suppress alarm?

indicators.note: powerless means without power, and P is power, so P comes out
to suppress something is to hold it down within, so the next piece goes inside

parts.note: easily influenced is pliant, and PLIANT loses P for power
an alarm bell, so an alarm is perhaps a bell

explanation.surface: A gullible fake-news outlet with no clout tries to keep a public alarm quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a propaganda outlet, but 'powerless' is an instruction: P is the abbreviation for power in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: A libellant is one who publishes a libel, a damaging falsehood in print, so fake news fits.

clue.text: Ignore new choice to install leader of Greens

indicators.note: to install something is to put it in place inside, so the next piece goes into the one before
the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
the elect are the chosen, the choice few
the first letter of Greens

explanation.surface: A political commentator urges voters to snub a new pick who would put the Green Party leader in office.
explanation.walkthrough: The leader of Greens reads as a party boss, but only the first letter is wanted. 'Choice' is ELECT as an adjective, the chosen few.
explanation.definitionFit: To neglect something is to pay it no attention, a plain synonym of ignore.

clue.text: Did peer briefly pierce through retired BBC grandee?

indicators.note: something passing through another runs inside it
to retire is to draw back, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: the BBC's top executive is the Director-General, DG, reversed
to lance a boil is to pierce it

explanation.surface: A question about whether a lord briefly skewered a retired BBC bigwig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a lord, as the grandee nearby suggests, but it is the verb to peer, to look. The BBC's chief is its Director-General.
explanation.definitionFit: To glance is to look briefly, so 'Did peer briefly' is the past tense glanced.

clue.text: Perhaps amount of toothpaste in bath one of you finally left

parts.note: a bath is a tub

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so each word gives only its last letter

parts.note: the last letters of onE oF yoU
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone complains that one of the household left the toothpaste in the bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One of you' reads as a finger pointed at a housemate, but it is three words each yielding its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothpaste comes in a tube, so a tubeful is one quantity of it; 'Perhaps' flags that toothpaste is only an example.

clue.text: German woman ultimately forgetting English past tense

parts.note: Frau is German for a married woman

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so each word gives its last letter

parts.note: the last letters of forgettinG englisH pasT

explanation.surface: A German woman who has forgotten her English past tenses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Past tense' looks like grammar, but the two words are split: 'past' is the last of the fodder and tense is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fraught means anxious and full of strain, as in a fraught meeting, a plain synonym of tense.

clue.text: Time off work each year starting late, ages to go

indicators.note: something starting late misses its opening, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: per annum, PA, means each year
ages is an eternity, and ETERNITY loses its first letter E
to leave is to go

explanation.surface: A worker's annual holiday is late starting and seems ages away.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface looks like it is all about the calendar, but the time off is a new father's. 'Each year' is the Latin per annum shrunk to PA.
explanation.definitionFit: Paternity leave is the break from work a father takes after his child is born, so it is a specific kind of time off.

clue.text: Where are we with getting organ for Women's Institute?

indicators.note: the word getting something receives it as a new part
one thing in exchange for another replaces it

parts.note: the ear is an organ of hearing
WITH once WI is taken out
WI, the Women's Institute, is the part swapped out

explanation.surface: A church organ is being bought for the Women's Institute, the British countrywomen's club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word, and it is the word being changed. The Women's Institute is a British organisation for rural women, known by its initials WI.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is our planet, so the answer to 'Where are we?' in the widest sense.

clue.text: American carrying bird book

indicators.note: in a down entry, the piece that carries another holds it up from below, so it comes second

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
US is short for American

explanation.surface: An American carrying a book about birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird book' reads as a field guide, but the two words are split: the bird is wordplay and the book is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus is a book of the New Testament, Paul's letter to Titus.

clue.text: Strand, in West End of metropolis, breaching intellectual property

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for west

indicators.note: to breach a wall is to break into it, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: IP is the usual abbreviation for intellectual property
the last letter of metropoliS

explanation.surface: The Strand, in London's West End, is the scene of an intellectual property breach.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a street in London's West End, so 'Strand', 'West End' and 'metropolis' all read as geography. 'West' and 'End of' belong to separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name a single fine thread of something, such as hair or smoke, so the two are plain synonyms.

clue.text: Hot dog that's nasty to get

parts.note: hot, meaning fashionable, is in
a cur is a nasty, snappish dog

explanation.surface: A hot dog so nasty you would rather not get one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot dog' is the fast food, but it splits: hot is fashionable, and the nasty dog is a cur. 'Get' here is the sense of getting a fine or a debt.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a penalty or a cost is to get it, usually unwillingly.

clue.text: Slothful mortal mostly regrets getting into Christianity to begin with

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: mortal means lethal, and LETHAL loses its last letter

indicators.note: what comes to begin with is at the front, so each word gives its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of Regrets Getting Into Christianity

explanation.surface: A lazy mortal who regrets coming late to religion.
explanation.walkthrough: Sloth is one of the seven deadly sins, which is why the surface drifts towards Christianity. 'Mortal' is the adjective, as in a mortal wound.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy, a straight synonym of slothful.

clue.text: Work of doctor, out of his depth, surprisingly succeeded

indicators.note: what turns out surprisingly is not what you expected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: HIS DEPTH rearranged
S is the standard abbreviation for succeeded

explanation.surface: A doctor who was out of his depth nevertheless succeeded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of his depth' is an idiom so solid you do not see 'out of' as a link, but it is: the answer is built out of HIS DEPTH. The doctor is an academic one, not a physician.
explanation.definitionFit: A PhD thesis is the dissertation written to earn a doctorate, so it is the work that makes a doctor.

clue.text: One teaching group of workers to run

parts.note: a trade union, TU, is a group of workers
used as it stands
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Someone teaching a workers' group how to run things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' is not a link word here but its own letters. A TU is a trade union, the British term for a labour union.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutor is a private or small-group teacher, so 'One teaching' is a plain description.
